title: Volatility
summary: Two positions of the same dollar size can move very differently. Volatility puts a scale on that difference.
body_markdown:
A $5,000 position tells you how much you have exposed to a market. It does not tell you how much that position usually moves. A quiet currency pair and a speculative stock can put very different amounts of capital at risk for the same notional exposure.


Volatility gives that second piece of information. It measures the size of price fluctuations over a specified period. It says little by itself about whether the next move will be up or down.


## Three measures of movement


Historical volatility is calculated from past returns. A common version measures their standard deviation: how widely individual returns vary around their average. A reading calculated from a month of daily closes describes a different sample from one calculated from a year of five-minute prices.


Average true range, or ATR, measures price ranges in the asset’s own units and includes gaps from the previous close. It is useful for asking whether a $2 stop is small or large relative to recent movement. It is not interchangeable with a percentage standard deviation.


Implied volatility comes from option prices. It describes the amount of future uncertainty being priced, including the price of bearing that uncertainty. For example,[CME’s CVOL indexes](https://www.cmegroup.com/market-data/cme-group-benchmark-administration/cme-group-volatility-indexes-faq.html) use options to estimate forward risk and express it in annualized terms. An implied figure is neither a direction forecast nor a guarantee of the movement that follows.


## From annual volatility to daily P&L


Suppose annualized volatility is 32%. For a simple illustration using 256 trading days, the usual square-root approximation gives:


**Daily volatility ≈ 32% ÷ √256 = 2%.**


A 2% move on $5,000 of linear exposure is $100. That gives a scale for ordinary daily fluctuation. The approximation assumes roughly stable volatility and uncorrelated returns across the periods being combined;[CME’s volatility lesson](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-options/discover-options-volatility) explains the time conversion. Using a different market calendar or measurement interval changes the calculation.


It would be a mistake to turn that $100 into a maximum loss. Volatility can rise abruptly, and returns need not follow a neat bell curve. An 8% earnings move would change the same position by $400. A one-day estimate also does not describe the worst path during the day: a market could fall sharply and recover before the close.


## Volatility and position size


Suppose a trade becomes unconvincing if price falls $2 and your planned loss before costs is $40. That supports 20 units. If a different setup needs $4 of room, the same loss budget supports 10 units.


**Units = planned dollar loss ÷ loss per unit.**


Recent volatility helps judge whether that invalidation point has room to mean anything. It should not become an excuse to move an existing exit farther away while leaving size unchanged. Wider room and smaller quantity belong in the same calculation.


There is a separate account question: can collateral support the price path? A long-term view may survive an 8% decline intellectually while a highly leveraged position cannot survive it financially. Financing and liquidation rules matter even if the eventual price forecast proves right.


## Events and liquidity


For an ordinary session, estimate the movement scale from relevant history. For a scheduled event, examine comparable event moves separately. Then consider what a larger gap would do to both the position and available margin.


Finally, inspect execution. A volatile market with substantial two-way trading can be easier to exit than a quiet market whose quotes vanish. Volatility measures movement; liquidity determines the price at which you can respond. The same expected price move can call for a smaller position when the exit is less reliable.
